Search-and-Explain

The builder types an area or a question and gets a priced, sourced answer with the evidence laid out — no map exploration required. It is the simplest, fastest route for someone who already knows the area they care about.

How it works

A single search box understands both plain-language questions ("what should I charge in Khalda?") and quick lookups ("Abdoun, 170 m², high finish"). It reads our real database, runs the same pricing engine the dashboard uses, and writes the answer back in plain words — with every number traceable to its source.

Example queries — and what comes back

The builder typesWhat the platform returns
"launch price for apartments in Khalda"Khalda's launch-price band (min-safe / recommended / premium) with a confidence level, the adjustment waterfall, and the comparable listings behind it — each sourced.
"compare Abdoun and Shmeisani"A side-by-side: recommended price, Investment Score, demand and competition for each — with the "why".
"170 m², floor 12, high finish, Abdoun"A priced result for that exact unit, adjusted for size / floor / finish, with the evidence for each adjustment.
"what can I pay for land in Dabouq?"The residual land value (max land price) worked from the recommended price minus construction, fees and profit — with the floor caveat.

When it's the faster choice & who it suits

  • The builder already knows the area and just wants the number and the proof
  • Quick, repeated lookups — check several known areas in a row
  • On a phone or a small screen, where a big map is awkward
  • Suits agents and analysts who work by name/address, not by browsing a map

Its limits

  • You have to know what to ask — it's weaker for open "where should I build?" discovery
  • Comparing many areas at once is less visual than a map
  • Terrain / view context (hills, surroundings) is harder to convey without the map
It complements the map, it doesn't replace it. Search is the fastest path when you know the area; the map (Approach A) is better for discovery. The two can live together — a search box on top of the map dashboard — and search is also a natural stepping-stone toward the AI co-pilot (Approach C).

Strengths

  • Simplest and fastest to use
  • Great for users who already know the area
  • Low learning curve — it's just a search box
  • Works well on any screen size, including mobile
  • A natural stepping-stone toward the AI co-pilot (Approach C)

Trade-offs

  • Less exploratory — you must know what to ask
  • Weaker for the "where should I build?" discovery step
  • Comparisons across many areas are less visual
  • Terrain / view context is harder to show without a map
